title: New theory reveals the possibility of extraterrestrial life existing throughout the universe.
excerpt: A new study by American and German scientists suggests that extraterrestrial life may exist in many places in the universe, challenging a long-held hypothesis.

A new study by American and German scientists suggests that extraterrestrial life may exist in many places in the universe, challenging a long-held hypothesis.

Editor's note

Extraterrestrial life has long been one of humanity's greatest mysteries, captivating the attention of all. Does life exist somewhere beyond our planets, and if so, what form do these beings take? From mysterious signals emanating from space to distant planets with conditions suitable for life, the search for extraterrestrial life continues to raise many questions that scientists are constantly seeking answers to.

Lesson 1: What would happen if humans found life beyond Earth?

Are humans alone in the universe?

Probably not. According to Popular Mechanics, a group of scientists believe that aliens may be living on other planets outside our solar system.

This idea is controversial because it contradicts a widely accepted hypothesis since 1983, which posits that intelligent life on Earth is the unique result of a series of unlikely circumstances that coincidentally converged in a way that is essentially a form of cosmic luck.

Instead, researchers argue that the evolutionary processes leading to the formation of intelligent life forms like humans are likely predictable outcomes, not only on our planet but also on other planets with extraterrestrial life.

According to the “hard steps” model of the evolution of intelligence, which originates from theories in the field of astrophysics, the likelihood of human evolution being successful is based on a series of “hard steps.” At its core, this hypothesis suggests that although life on a planet needs a nearby star to provide energy, the time it takes for humans to evolve on Earth compared to the total lifespan of the Sun suggests that the emergence of humanity is highly unlikely. The “hard steps” model also predicts why intelligent life seems to be rare in the universe.

However, researchers at the University of Munich in Germany, Pennsylvania State University, and the University of Rochester in the United States have published a study that challenges this view. Their interdisciplinary model combines knowledge from astrophysics, geology, paleontology, and biology to provide a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of how life emerged and evolved on a planet like Earth. The research team published their results in February 2025 in the journal Science Advances.

Revealing how extraterrestrial life emerged.

Instead of relying on the Sun's lifespan for explanation, researchers suggest that the emergence of humans and other intelligent life forms in the universe may be a natural result of changes in the planet's environmental factors. These factors include sea surface temperature, ocean salinity, and atmospheric oxygen levels, all of which are conditions that influence life.

According to research, at different points in Earth's history, the combination of various environmental factors has opened up "windows" of opportunity for life to evolve and thrive.

Dr. Jennifer Macalady, an Earth scientist at Pennsylvania State University and co-author of the study, noted: "This alternative model suggests that the evolution of complex life may not depend so much on luck, but primarily on the interaction between life and its environment. This opens up promising new avenues of research in our quest to understand our origins and humanity's place in the universe."

In other words, humans may not have needed “a series of lucky breaks” to appear and survive to this day, according to Dr. Dan Mills, a researcher at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and lead author of the study. Mills suggests that humans appeared “at the right time in terms of our planet’s development, and that other planets may have reached these conditions faster than Earth, while some others may have needed more time.”

Researchers plan to test the new model in several ways. For example, searching the atmospheres of exoplanets could help detect biological signatures, such as the presence of oxygen. This could be an indicator of the existence of life forms that produce or consume oxygen.

On Earth, the abundant oxygen that supported multicellular life only emerged after populations of cyanobacteria flourished about 2.5 billion years ago and produced oxygen. A similar process may be underway elsewhere in the universe.

Scientists also want to test the “hard steps” model itself by placing single-celled and multicellular life forms in extreme environmental conditions, such as lower oxygen concentrations and temperatures, to see if they can adapt. It's possible that how these organisms react will show that even the “hard steps” model of life isn't as difficult as previously thought.

Otherwise, this result could become another argument in support of the hypothesis that life, even intelligent life like humans, has appeared multiple times throughout the universe.
